Bequeath

/bih-KWEETH/ - rhymes with beneath · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Bequeath means to leave something to someone through a will.

The comedian bequeathed his notebooks to the colleague who had opened for him for thirty years, with instructions to steal only the best jokes.

Worked Example

Old Marta the blacksmith let her apprentice borrow the good anvil but never gave it away. The forge, the tongs, the anvil, and the little book of hammer notes stayed hers until her will was read, when all of it passed, exactly as she had put it in writing, to the apprentice who had swept her floor for nine years.

Bequeath is the exact word for what Marta did, because it means to leave something to someone through a will — the handover waits for the will to be read. Hand down comes close, but a grandmother can hand down a ring on any birthday; bequeath keeps the lawyer, the paper, and the waiting in the picture.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hand down: pass to the next generation — will or no will

leave: the everyday word for the same act; a will 'leaves' things in plain speech

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disinherit: strike someone out of the will

keep back: hold on to what someone hoped to receive

Where it sits · how much legal formality the transfer involves — give → hand down → bequeath

give vs. bequeath: Give is the everyday floor — a sandwich, a pencil, no paperwork and no waiting.

hand down vs. bequeath: To hand something down goes further than to give it — a younger generation is implied — but it can happen at any birthday, while bequeath waits for the reading of a will.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — be-

Prefix — be-: thoroughly, about (Old English)

Root — queath

Root — queath: to say, to declare (Old English cwethan)

Put it together

Put it together: Be- (thoroughly) + queath (to say, declare) = to declare formally. Old English becwethan was to 'speak' your property to someone — a will was said aloud before it was written down. The old verb survives almost nowhere else; the raven's 'quoth' in storybooks is its last cousin standing.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: The Old English verb cwethan, 'to say,' died out of daily speech centuries ago — only the storybook 'quoth' and the legal noun bequest keep its shape. Bequeath is a fossil: a word for saying who gets what, outliving the verb it was built on.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / legal

Bequeath belongs to wills: it is how a benefactor gives one final time, on paper, effective at death. For a ring passed across the dinner table, hand down is the honest word; keep bequeath for the lawyer's office. Largess and munificence, its unit-mates, describe giving the giver is alive to enjoy.
